related_questions.question: What is the best bankruptcy for individuals?
related_questions.snippet: Chapter 7 bankruptcy is faster and cheaper than Chapter 13. Chapter 7 bankruptcy discharges, or erases, eligible debts such as credit card bills, medical debt and personal loans. But other debts, such as student loans and taxes, typically are harder to get discharged.
related_questions.title: Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 Bankruptcy: What Is the Difference? - NerdWallet

text_blocks.snippet: Chapter 7 bankruptcy is the type that typically clears the most debt, often referred to as a "fresh start" bankruptcy. It involves liquidating some assets to pay off creditors, and the remaining eligible debt is then discharged. However, it's important to understand that not all debts are discharged in bankruptcy, and some obligations, like certain taxes and student loans, usually survive the process.

list.title: Liquidation:
list.snippet: Chapter 7 involves selling non-exempt assets to pay creditors. However, many filers can keep most of their assets due to exemptions.

list.title: Discharge:
list.snippet: Once the liquidation process is complete, the court issues a discharge order, which releases the debtor from the legal obligation to repay most of the remaining unsecured debts.

list.title: Eligible Debts:
list.snippet: Chapter 7 typically discharges debts like credit card balances, medical bills, personal loans, and some utility bills.

list.title: Ineligible Debts:
list.snippet: Certain debts, like most taxes, student loans, child support, and alimony, are generally not discharged in Chapter 7.

list.title: Means Test:
list.snippet: To qualify for Chapter 7, filers usually need to pass a means test, which assesses their income and expenses to determine if they can afford to repay their debts.

list.title: Timeframe:
list.snippet: Chapter 7 bankruptcy cases are typically completed within a few months.

list.title: Automatic Stay:
list.snippet: Filing Chapter 7 triggers an automatic stay, which temporarily halts most collection actions from creditors.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, while Chapter 7 bankruptcy can eliminate a significant amount of debt, it's crucial to understand that certain debts are not dischargeable and to determine if you qualify for this type of bankruptcy.

related_questions.question: What is best to file bankruptcy?

text_blocks.snippet: The "best" bankruptcy chapter to file (Chapter 7 or Chapter 13) depends on individual circumstances, primarily income, assets, and the nature of the debts. Chapter 7 is generally faster and cheaper, and suitable for those with low income and few assets, while Chapter 13 allows for repayment plans and potentially saving a home from foreclosure, but is more complex and costly.

list.title: Best for:
list.snippet: Individuals with low income and limited assets, predominantly unsecured debts like credit card bills and medical expenses, and those who don't own a home with significant equity.

list.title: Process:
list.snippet: Involves liquidating non-exempt assets to pay creditors, but most Chapter 7 filers keep all their property due to exemptions.

list.title: Pros:
list.snippet: Quicker and less expensive than Chapter 13.

list.title: Cons:
list.snippet: May not be suitable for those with substantial income or valuable assets, and can impact credit score.

list.title: Best for:
list.snippet: Individuals with regular income who can propose a repayment plan to pay off debts over 3-5 years, especially those facing foreclosure or wanting to protect valuable assets.

list.title: Process:
list.snippet: Involves developing a repayment plan to pay creditors over time, potentially including catching up on missed mortgage payments.

list.title: Pros:
list.snippet: Allows individuals to keep their assets, potentially save their home, and repay debts over time.

list.title: Cons:
list.snippet: More complex and costly than Chapter 7, and requires a consistent income to make payments.

list.title: Income:
list.snippet: Chapter 7 has an income test; if your income is too high, you may not qualify.

list.title: Assets:
list.snippet: Chapter 7 involves liquidating non-exempt assets; consider whether you can protect your property under exemptions.

list.title: Debts:
list.snippet: Chapter 7 may not be suitable for all types of debt, especially those that are not dischargeable (e.g., student loans, taxes).

list.title: Goals:
list.snippet: Consider whether you want a quick debt discharge or a longer-term repayment plan to save your home.

text_blocks.snippet: It is crucial to consult with a bankruptcy attorney or a credit counseling agency to assess your specific situation and determine the most appropriate bankruptcy chapter for your circumstances, according to NerdWallet and LegalZoom.
